extracted.intended_audience: police administrators, policymakers, and general readers interested in frontier policing and the history/administration of the Royal North-West Mounted Police
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, practices, and administrative recommendations for policing a vast frontier territory (early Royal North-West Mounted Police): force size, training, investigative methods, public relations, and limits on police duties. Drawn from Commissioner reports and officers' accounts in a historical chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sufficient force strength and reserves
rubrics_metrics.description: The Force should be of adequate size to match population and territory demands; Commissioner Perry urged maintenance of a sufficiently large force and specifically advocated 'a reserve of at least fifty men always in training' at headquarters to be qualified for detachment duty whenever occasion arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: with expanding population and widening areas the strain on corps increases; a reserve ensures detachments can be filled with experienced, trained men without overworking those already on duty. Quote: 'The Commissioner therefore strongly urged not only the maintenance of a sufficiently large force... but pressed for the adoption of his particular policy to have a reserve of at least fifty men always in training at headquarters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough depot training before detached duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Men must receive thorough groundwork training in the depot division before being sent on detached duty; untested recruits should not be assigned to responsible positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit prohibition on sending men who 'have not the proper qualifications, necessary experience, and who have not yet established a reputation for reliability and sobriety.' Training ensures they can act on their own initiative and advise settlers; 'it is therefore unwise... to send on detached duty men who have not the proper qualifications.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select men of good character, reliability, and sobriety
rubrics_metrics.description: Personnel selection criteria emphasize good character, proven reliability, sobriety, and prior testing—essential for detached and responsible positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner argues detached men must be 'well trained, have experience, and be of good character' and must be 'tested and proved' before detachment. Recruitment and promotion should factor in these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control, discipline, and tact to minimize violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Policing should prioritize avoidance of avoidable shooting; officers must be self-controlled, disciplined and tactful, using restraint to keep the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: 'Their business was to keep avoidable shooting off the programme altogether... they must be self-controlled, disciplined and tactful men.' Training and esprit de corps should emphasize de-escalation and measured conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and discreet management of sensitive disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with communal or religious disputes, police should not take sides but maintain balance, keep the peace, and use minimal intervention to avoid inflaming passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Superintendent Constantine locked the church and had rival parties hold separate services outside rather than interfering between priests; 'Constantine would not interfere as between the controversialists, but he kept his eye on the situation and gave special direction to certain of his men.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Close oversight of travellers and rapid communication between posts
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain tight surveillance and rapid information flows so that travellers cannot 'disappear' without swift inquiry: wire communications and patrols should be used to trace missing persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meticulous, imaginative, and persistent investigative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should be exhaustive and inventive—careful scene scrutiny, preservation of small physical clues, piecing circumstantial evidence, following trails, and persistence across jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Corporal Pennecuick's examination of tree stumps (axe nick patterns), sweeping trails for drag marks, recovery of bullets and personal effects, use of dogs to track, matching bills and curios to victims, and assembling exhibits to produce compact circumstantial evidence. The account emphasizes attention to minor details and methodical collection/analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to expend resources to enforce the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities should permit (and be prepared for) substantial expense in serious investigations and prosecutions to ensure justice and deterrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the O'Brien case 'ran up a bill of over $100,000' but yielded reputational and deterrent benefits; Commissioner notes such expenditure is an investment in settlement and security—'a splendid investment which will pay big dividends to the country for generations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible watchfulness and patrol presence as crime prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant, visible watchfulness by police deters 'loose characters' and makes it difficult for criminals to operate undetected in mining and frontier regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspector reports attribute low serious crime to 'the extreme watchfulness of our men which renders it well nigh impossible for loose characters to engage in doubtful enterprises and stay in the country.' Therefore patrols, posts and visibility are central prevention measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage self-reliance among settlers; limit police responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Police should not be expected to assume tasks that are the settlers' responsibility (e.g., recovering stray horses); while police will investigate and circulate descriptions, settlers must take precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspector Wilson rebukes settlers who expect the Force to hunt up lost horses; the Force forwards descriptions and notifies detachments, but cannot substitute for owners' reasonable precautions. This delineates limits on service and promotes shared responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of procedural measures to ensure proper identification and estate handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When bodies are found or deaths occur, hold inquests and take steps to identify remains so that estates and other legal matters are not confused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Inspector Wroughton held an inquest to identify Dr. Bettinger 'so that any matters connected with the estate might not be confused.' Formal procedures and inquests are part of administrative policing duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good public relations, courtesy, and civil duties beyond law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Police should provide courteous escorts for dignitaries, render humane acts (rescuing the insane, assisting communities), and cultivate public confidence and attachment across communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: escorts for Governors-General and royalty; Corporal Field's 1,300-mile humane escort of an insane man; the respectful funeral and cross-border recognition of a drowned constable. Such acts enhance the Force's reputation and social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair recognition and reward for service
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper and timely recognition (medals, honors) should be given to service members for meritorious or wartime service to avoid past injustices and to maintain morale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: delayed granting of medals to Mounted Police who served in the North-West Rebellion of 1885—'These men deserved the medal and should have had it at the outset, but better late than never.' Administrative fairness in honors is a standard.
